paragraphs: It took the Lady a few moments to convince herself that something really was happening in the corner of the room. Even then, what it was remained far from clear.
“To put it as mildly as possible,” she murmured, “this is bordering on the uncanny.” Leaning forward over her silk-covered knees, she watched the phenomenon.

At first it had seemed like a faint, unexplained disturbance in the air, apparently caused by neither an open window nor a door. Some papers fluttered to the floor, and the fringes of the curtains stirred softly. It would still have been easy to dismiss it as a wandering draught, if things had not suddenly become unmistakably unusual. All the air in the room seemed to rush violently towards that one point. There it underwent what struck her as a convulsion of the air. At the very centre and source of it, in the confusion, something almost resembling a shape seemed to appear from time to time.

The room’s silence was broken by a book flying open, its pages fluttering; by the sound of a vase of violets blowing over, its scented water dripping onto the floor; and by soft touches all around, as though a breeze were passing through a room full of little ornaments.

The Lady’s curls were swept forward towards the corner she was watching. There, the air had become so tense with something about to happen, so torn by some unimaginable struggle, that she rose without thinking. Stepping forward against the pressure of her petticoats, which blew around her ankles, she impatiently thrust her hand into the——

At once she felt another hand take hers, though its grasp was far from solid. For another moment, what she saw before her trembled between something and nothing. Then, from that uncertain state, the figure of a young man slowly emerged into doubtful view. He wore evening clothes, with a cloak draped over them in generous folds—the kind worn by fashionable ghosts.
“The devil was in it!” he complained. “I thought I would never materialise.”
She threw herself into her chair, bewildered. Yet even in the shock of the moment, she remained true to herself and did not forget to smooth her disordered curls.
Her visitor had been looking himself over with dissatisfaction. Now he exclaimed irritably, “Forgive me, my dear, but are my feet on the floor, or where on earth are they?”

In a reassuring tone, she admitted that his patent-leather shoes were a mere two or three inches above the rug. With another effort, he lowered himself until his feet rested properly on the floor. Only when he walked around to examine the ornaments was there a suspicious lightness in his step.

Once this inspection had settled his nerves, he approached the Lady. He had carried it out with a great air of casual indifference, which nevertheless failed to hide the fact that his heart was beating rather wildly.

“Well, here we are again, my love!” he cried, covering her hands with ghostly kisses. “It seems an eternity since I began struggling back to you through the outer void and all the rest of it. Sometimes, I admit, I almost despaired. Life for those without bodies is not all pleasure and games, I assure you.”
He drew a long breath. His gaze seemed to enfold and cherish both her and the whole room.

“Little room, little room! So this is what you are like! Do you know,” he went on eagerly, “I wondered about you in the grave. I could hardly sleep, knowing I had never entered this place. Ah, me! How much we leave undone! My passion for literature was strong, and I dashed this off at the time:

“Now everything is done, and I lie so low,
I cannot sleep for this, my one regret:
Though I could never know that shadowed place,
I never went where my heart longed to go,
Or saw you sitting there in thought!
“Well, well, these things trouble a ghost so much. Naturally, I came back as soon as I could—to be sure—to be sure that you were still mine.” He fixed her with a piercing look.

“I see from the calendar on your writing table that some years have passed since I——um——since I died,” he added with a faint blush. It seems that well-bred ghosts tend to keep the subject of their death out of conversation.
“Ah, me! How time flies! You’ll be joining me soon, my dear.”
She drew herself up magnificently. He became aware of her beauty, still holding on to all its excellence; of the delicate insolence of Life looking at Death; of the fact that she had forgotten him.

He stood to face this, his trembling hands thrust into his pockets, then turned away to hide his dismay. But he was a ghost with considerable spirit, and in a moment he rose to the occasion. Under her blank, indignant gaze, he took a card from his case. Borrowing a pencil from the writing desk, he wrote beneath the name:

“Peace to the breast,
Wherever it may be,
That gave an hour’s rest
To the heart of me.
Peace to the breast
Until it lies dead,
And the heart is clay
Where I once stayed.
Peace to the breast,
Though it quite forgets
The guest it once sheltered;
To the heart, good night!”
He handed her the card and bowed. Then, from habit, he turned to the door, forgetting that his ghostly hand could not turn the knob.

When the door did not open, he sighed, remembering his ghostly condition, and prepared to disappear. He cast one last look at the faithless Lady. She was still looking at the card in her hand, and tears were running down her face.

“She has remembered,” he thought. “How polite!” For a moment he seemed able to contain his disappointment and withdraw discreetly, feeling that he had reached the moment for vanishing, with the customary reserve of the dead. But emotion overcame him. In an instant he had her in his arms. He poured out his love, his reproaches, the story of his longing, his doubts, his unhappiness, and his desperate journey back to earth to see her. “And ah!” he cried, “imagine my agony when I found that you had forgotten. Yet I suspected it in the darkness. My restlessness and despair told me. Perhaps a few lines that came to me will give you some idea—you remember my old knack for verse?

“Where the grasses weep
Over his darkened bed,
And the glow-worms creep,
Lies the weary head
Of one buried deep, who cannot sleep:
The unremembered dead.”

He sat beside her and spoke of their old love for each other, of his faithfulness through every change. Along the way he spoke of her beauty, her cruelty, the light of her face that had lit his dark journey towards her—and many other things. The Lady bowed her head and wept.

The hours of the night passed like this. The moon faded, and the dark cheek of the east began to turn pale. Still his eloquence flowed on, while the Lady clasped his misty hands to her breast, her love reawakened. At last a hint of pink touched the curtain. He rose abruptly.
“I cannot hold out against the morning,” he said. “It is time all good ghosts were in bed.”
But she fell to her knees before him and clasped his insubstantial waist in a desperate embrace.
“Oh, do not leave me,” she cried, “or my love will kill me!”
He bent eagerly over her. “Say it again—convince me!”
“I love you,” she cried, again and again and again, with such painful sincerity that she would have convinced the most sceptical ghost ever to revisit the moonlit world.
“You will forget again,” he said.

“I will never forget!” she cried. “From now on, my life will be one continual remembrance of you, one long act of devotion to your memory, one offering, one unending repentance, one agony of waiting!”
He lifted her face and saw that it was true.
“Well,” he said, wrapping his cloak gracefully around him, “well, now I shall have a little peace.”
With a certain jaunty grace, he kissed her hair and prepared to dissolve, lightly tapping a rhythm against his leg with the dove-grey gloves he carried.
“Goodbye, my dear!” he said. “Now I shall sleep at night. My heart is quite at rest.”
“But mine is breaking,” she wailed, frantically trying once more to clasp his vanishing form.
He blew her a kiss from his misty fingertips. All that remained with her, besides her broken heart, was a faint disturbance in the air.
